raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old male patient, farmer by occupation, presented to the orthopedic outpatient department with the complaint of painful gluteal mass with restricted hip movement for the past 12 years. He had undergone incision and drainage on couple of occasions at a local health-care center. On both of those occasions after a brief period of symptomatic relief, painful swelling reoccurred. On physical examination, a large cystic swelling associated with pain and reduced hip movement was observed over the left gluteal region. With the suspicion of osteoarticular tuberculosis, he had undergone antitubercular therapy without any symptomatic relief from the local hospital. Thus, osteoarticular tuberculosis was kept much lower as a differential diagnosis in this case.
Plain radiograph revealed reduced joint space and cystic lesion with destruction of ischial tuberosity, acetabulum, and femoral head [Figure 1]. Other routine investigations revealed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and eosinophilia with absolute eosinophil count of 730/ml. Renal and liver function tests were found to be under normal range.
Serum sample was received by the department of microbiology for hydatid serology to rule out possible parasitic infection. Hydatid serology using immunoglobulin G (IgG) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (RIDASCREEN Echinococcus IgG, R-Biopharm AG, Germany) was performed following the manufacturer's instruction, and surprisingly, the optical density value was above the cutoff. Hydatid serology result was further correlated with computer tomography scan (CT-scan) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis. CT-scan and MRI revealed a multiloculated cyst with destruction of left ischial tuberosity, acetabulum, and femoral head. Few calcified foci were also noted supporting positive hydatid serology.
Based on the above serological and radiological findings, a provisional diagnosis of primary pelvic hydatidosis was made. Surgery was planned and the patient underwent preoperative albendazole chemotherapy, followed by en bloc mass excision of the cyst without rupturing the cyst wall. The removed tissue with a cyst was sent to the department of pathology for histopathological analysis. Hematoxylin and eosin stainingrevealed a thick cyst wall with few daughter cysts, occasional calcified foci with intense inflammatory responses, and exuberant giant cell reaction against lamellated membranes [Figures 2 and 3] consistent with hydatid cyst. Postoperative period was uneventful and was subsequently discharged with advice of albendazole (10 mg/kg) chemotherapy for 3 months with a regular follow-up. During his last follow-up, the patient had no fresh complaints. He had better hip movement without pain and was walking with support.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male farmer presented with a 12-year history of a recurrent painful left gluteal mass and restricted left hip movement.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced a painful left gluteal swelling and progressive restriction of left hip motion over 12 years. He had previously undergone incision and drainage on two occasions at a local clinic (followed by recurrence) as well as empirical anti-tuberculous therapy for suspected osteoarticular tuberculosis without lasting relief.
subjective.past_medical_history: Two prior local incision and drainage procedures and empirical anti-tuberculous therapy; worked as a farmer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic left gluteal pain, recurrent gluteal swelling, and restricted hip motion.

objective.physical_examination: A large, painful cystic swelling over the left gluteal region accompanied by restricted left hip range of motion.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed elevated ESR, elevated CRP, and peripheral eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count 730/mL [730/uL]), with normal renal and liver function tests. Serum Echinococcus IgG ELISA (RIDASCREEN) was positive above the cutoff. Plain pelvic radiograph showed reduced left hip joint space and osteolytic cystic destruction of the left ischial tuberosity, acetabulum, and femoral head.
objective.advanced_workup: Pelvic CT and MRI demonstrated a multiloculated cystic mass with focal calcifications causing extensive osteolytic destruction of the left ischial tuberosity, acetabulum, and femoral head. Following preoperative albendazole therapy and en bloc surgical excision without cyst rupture, H&E histopathology revealed a thick cyst wall with daughter cysts, calcified foci, and an exuberant foreign-body giant cell reaction against acellular lamellated membranes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary pelvic and coxofemoral osteoarticular hydatidosis (involving the left ischial tuberosity, acetabulum, and femoral head), confirmed by positive RIDASCREEN Echinococcus IgG ELISA and histopathological identification of daughter cysts and lamellated membranes (ruling out osteoarticular tuberculosis). Treated with preoperative oral albendazole, intact en bloc surgical excision, and 3 months of postoperative albendazole (10 mg/kg/day), achieving pain-free assisted ambulation and improved hip mobility on follow-up.
